listening.title: Six hours in Istanbul

speakers.Julian: a young lawyer from Baku who plans everything
speakers.Yunus: his friend, a potter who prefers to go with the flow

listening.direction: Two old friends talking in a busy airport café in Istanbul at 6 a.m. Natural, unscripted feel: overlaps, small hesitations, real laughter. Background: soft announcements, cups. Not a textbook recording.

lines.t: [yawns] Six in the morning. Six. And you've already had two coffees.
Three. But who's counting? Look, we have a six-hour layover, and I made a plan.
Of course you made a plan. [laughs] Let me see... Julian, this is a whole page.

It's an itinerary. It's different. So — first, we take the metro to Sultanahmet, that's forty minutes. Then the Blue Mosque, then the Grand Bazaar, then lunch by the water, and then back here by eleven-thirty.
Eleven-thirty. And our flight to London is at...?
Twelve-fifteen.
[slowly] Forty-five minutes. For customs, security, finding the gate...
Okay, okay — maybe eleven. I'll fix it.
Can I say something? Every time you travel, you come home more tired than when you left.
That's not true. [pause] That's... a little bit true.
Remember Rome? You saw nine churches in one day and you couldn't remember any of them.
[laughs] I remember the third one. It had a nice door.
A nice door. Great. So here's my plan. We take the metro, yes. But then we just walk. No list. We find a small street, off the beaten track, somewhere with good tea and no tour groups.
And if we get lost?
Then we ask someone. People here are friendly. That's the best part of travelling — talking to people, not taking photos of buildings.
Hmm. But we're only here once. Don't you want to see the famous places?
The famous places will be here next year. This morning won't.
[sighs] That sounds like something you read on a tea bag.
[laughs] Maybe. But it's still true.
Fine. Compromise. One famous place, then your little streets. And we're back here at ten-thirty. Not eleven. Ten-thirty.
Deal. And Julian? Leave the big bag in a locker. Travel light for once.
My laptop is in that bag.
Exactly. [laughs] Come on, let's hit the road before you make another list.

questions.q: What is the main disagreement between Julian and Yunus?
questions.why: Julian wants a full plan of famous places; Yunus wants to walk freely.

questions.q: How long is their layover?
questions.why: Julian says: "We have a six-hour layover."

questions.q: Why does Yunus mention Rome?
options: Julian saw too much and remembered almost nothing
questions.why: Julian saw nine churches in one day and couldn't remember them.

questions.q: What does Yunus mean by "The famous places will be here next year. This morning won't"?
options: They should come back next year
Enjoy the moment — it won't happen again
They don't have enough time to see anything
questions.why: He means the experience of this morning is special and won't repeat.

questions.q: In the end, what do they agree to do?
options: See one famous place, then walk the small streets
questions.why: Julian's compromise: one famous place, then Yunus's little streets.

voiceDirection.Julian: Late twenties, Baku lawyer. Warm, a little anxious, over-plans everything. Speaks fast when nervous, laughs at himself.
voiceDirection.Yunus: Early thirties, potter and chess player. Relaxed, slow, dry humour, teases Julian like an older brother.

A2.text:
Julian lives in Baku. He works a lot, and he does not travel often. Last spring, he had a holiday in Georgia with his friend Yunus.

Julian made a plan for every day. He wrote the times of the trains, the names of the museums and the cafés in a small notebook. Yunus laughed at the notebook. "You don't need a plan," he said. "You need good shoes."

On the third day, they wanted to go from Tbilisi to a small town in the mountains. Julian checked his notebook and they got on a train. After one hour, Julian looked out of the window. There were no mountains. There was the sea.

"Yunus," he said, "I think this is the wrong train."

They got off at a small station. There was no café, only an old woman selling bread and cheese. She did not speak English, and they did not speak Georgian. But she smiled, gave them tea and drew a map on a piece of paper.

They waited three hours for the next train. They ate bread, drank tea and played chess on Yunus's phone. Julian did not look at his notebook once.

Later, Julian told everyone about the holiday. He did not talk about the museums. He talked about the wrong train.

B1.text:
Julian is the kind of traveller who checks the weather a week before a trip and packs his suitcase three days early. So when his friend Yunus suggested a spring holiday in Georgia, Julian spent two evenings building the perfect itinerary: train times, museum opening hours, even the name of the café where they would have breakfast each morning.

Yunus, who prefers to travel light and decide things on the day, found the notebook hilarious. "You've planned so much," he said, "that there's no room left for anything to happen."

For two days, the plan worked perfectly. Then, on the third morning, they rushed onto a train they believed was going to Kazbegi, in the mountains. An hour later, Julian noticed something strange. The view outside was getting flatter, not higher, and in the distance he could see the grey line of the sea.

They got off at the next stop, a tiny station with one bench and no timetable. The only person there was an elderly woman selling bread and cheese from a basket. Communication was difficult — a mix of Russian, gestures and laughter — but she understood their problem immediately. She poured them tea from a flask, drew a careful map on the back of a paper bag and told them the next train would come "maybe in three hours".

At first Julian was annoyed. Half a day of his plan was gone. But slowly, something changed. They shared her bread, watched farmers working in the fields and played chess on a broken bench. By the time the train finally arrived, Julian realised he hadn't checked the time once.

Back in Baku, colleagues asked him about the trip. He tried to describe the famous monastery, but the story he kept telling was about the wrong train, the paper-bag map and the woman with the flask.

questions.q: What does the first paragraph tell us about Julian?
options: He travels a lot for work
questions.why: He checks the weather a week early and packs three days early.

questions.q: What does Yunus mean by "there's no room left for anything to happen"?
questions.why: He thinks a full plan leaves no space for unexpected experiences.

questions.q: How did Julian realise they were on the wrong train?
options: The land became flatter and he saw the sea
His phone showed the wrong city
The train stopped for a long time
questions.why: "The view was getting flatter... he could see the sea."

questions.q: The woman spoke good English. True, false or not given?
questions.why: They communicated with Russian, gestures and laughter.

questions.q: How did Julian's feelings change at the station?
questions.why: At first he was annoyed, then he stopped checking the time.

B2.text:
There are two kinds of travellers, Julian once read: those who collect places and those who collect moments. For most of his adult life he had belonged firmly to the first group. A trip, for him, was a project to be managed — a series of famous sights to be visited, photographed and ticked off a list. So when his friend Yunus proposed a week in Georgia, Julian responded the way he always did: with a spreadsheet.

Yunus, a potter who measures time in the hours it takes clay to dry, was openly amused. "You've scheduled breakfast," he pointed out. "Do you also schedule being hungry?" Julian laughed, but kept the spreadsheet.

The first two days went exactly as planned, which, looking back, was precisely the problem: Julian remembered them as a blur of queues and ticket offices. On the third morning, in their hurry to catch a train to Kazbegi, they jumped onto the wrong platform. It took Julian almost an hour to notice that the mountains he had been promised were stubbornly refusing to appear, and that the horizon ahead was unmistakably the sea.

They abandoned the train at a station so small it seemed to exist only out of habit. Its sole occupant was an elderly woman with a basket of bread and cheese, who assessed their situation with a single glance. Without a common language, she nevertheless managed to communicate everything that mattered: that they were lost, that this was not a disaster, and that tea would help. She sketched a remarkably precise map on a paper bag and estimated, with a shrug, that the next train might come in three hours.

Julian's first instinct was to calculate what the delay had cost him — a museum, a viewpoint, a carefully chosen lunch. But somewhere between the second cup of tea and a surprisingly competitive game of chess, the calculation stopped mattering. For the first time on the trip, he was not on his way to somewhere else.

Months later, when colleagues asked about Georgia, Julian noticed that he could barely describe the monastery he had travelled so far to see. Yet he could still picture every line of that paper-bag map. Perhaps, he admitted to Yunus, he had been collecting the wrong things all along.

questions.q: What is the main idea of the text?
options: Unplanned moments can matter more than famous sights
Yunus is a better planner than Julian
questions.why: Julian ends up valuing the moment at the station over the monastery.

questions.q: Why does the writer say the first two days going to plan "was precisely the problem"?
questions.why: Julian remembers them only "as a blur of queues and ticket offices".

questions.q: "A station so small it seemed to exist only out of habit" suggests the station was…
questions.why: It was so small and empty it seemed to have no real purpose.

questions.q: The woman spoke some Georgian and some English. True, false or not given?
questions.why: They had no common language.

questions.q: What does Julian mean by "collecting the wrong things all along"?
questions.why: It links back to "those who collect places and those who collect moments".
